title: Ecology — Concepts and Ecosystems
topicTitle: Ecosystem ecology: concept of ecology, biotic and abiotic factors, species interactions; concept of ecosystem, structural and functional aspects of pond and forest ecosystem
notes: **Ecology — definition and scope:** Ecology is the scientific study of interactions between organisms and their environment. It examines how biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) factors shape the distribution, abundance, behaviour, and evolution of organisms. Ecology spans from individual adaptations to global biogeochemical cycles, operating across spatial scales from a rotting log to the entire biosphere.

**Levels of ecological organisation:** Organism (individual physiology and behaviour) → Population (group of same species in an area) → Community (all interacting populations in an area) → Ecosystem (community plus abiotic environment) → Biome (major regional community types defined by climate) → Biosphere (all ecosystems on Earth). Each level exhibits emergent properties not predictable from the level below.

**Biotic factors — producers (autotrophs):** Organisms that synthesise organic compounds from inorganic sources using sunlight (photosynthesis) or chemical energy (chemosynthesis). In ecosystems, primary producers form the base of all food chains. Terrestrial producers include trees, grasses, and shrubs; aquatic producers include phytoplankton, algae, and aquatic plants. Producers convert approximately 1-3% of incident solar energy into chemical energy.

**Biotic factors — consumers (heterotrophs):** Herbivores (primary consumers) feed on producers; carnivores (secondary consumers) feed on herbivores; tertiary consumers feed on carnivores; omnivores feed on multiple trophic levels. Decomposers (fungi, bacteria) and detritivores (earthworms, millipedes) break down dead organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the ecosystem. Scavengers (vultures, hyenas) consume dead animals.

**Abiotic factors — physical and chemical:** Temperature controls enzyme activity and metabolic rates — most organisms function within 0-40°C. Light intensity and quality (red:blue ratio) determine photosynthetic rates and influence flowering time (photoperiodism). Water availability (precipitation, humidity, soil moisture) is the primary determinant of biome distribution. Soil pH affects nutrient solubility; most plants prefer 6.0-7.5. Dissolved oxygen in water limits aquatic respiration.

**Pond ecosystem — structural components:** Biotic: phytoplankton (diatoms, green algae), rooted macrophytes (lotus, hydrilla), zooplankton (Daphnia, rotifers), insects (dragonfly nymphs, water beetles), fish (roach, carp), amphibians (frogs, newts), birds (herons, ducks), bacteria and fungi. Abiotic: water column (temperature stratification in summer), sediment (organic detritus, clay), dissolved gases (O2, CO2), mineral nutrients (nitrates, phosphates), light penetration (euphotic zone extends to ~2m in clear ponds).

**Pond ecosystem — functional processes:** Energy flow: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish → decomposers. Nutrient cycling: detritus is broken down by bacteria and fungi; nutrients are taken up by algae and plants; herbivores consume producers; waste and dead matter return to sediment for decomposition. Seasonal succession: ponds naturally progress from open water → marginal vegetation → swamp → meadow → forest through sedimentation and plant succession over centuries.

**Forest ecosystem — structural components:** Vertical stratification: emergent layer (tallest trees above canopy), canopy (continuous layer of crowns, 80% of forest biodiversity), understory (shade-tolerant trees and shrubs), shrub layer, herb layer, forest floor (leaf litter, decomposers). Root structure: shallow fibrous roots vs. deep taproots. Soil layers: O (organic), A (topsoil), B (subsoil), C (parent material), R (bedrock). Canopy gaps (from fallen trees) create patches of high light driving regeneration.

**Forest ecosystem — functional processes:** Primary production: tropical rainforests have the highest NPP (~2,200 g/m2/year) of any biome. Carbon sequestration: forests store ~662 billion tonnes of carbon in biomass and soils. Transpiration: trees release water vapour, generating cloud cover and rainfall (biotic pump theory). Mycorrhizal networks (wood wide web): fungal hyphae connect tree roots, enabling nutrient exchange and chemical signalling between trees. Decomposition is rapid in tropics (weeks) but slow in boreal forests (years).

**Ecological pyramids:** Pyramid of numbers — counts individuals at each trophic level (can be inverted: one oak tree supports thousands of insects). Pyramid of biomass — total dry mass at each level (can be inverted in aquatic systems: phytoplankton biomass < zooplankton biomass at any instant). Pyramid of energy — always upright because energy is lost as heat at each transfer (2nd law of thermodynamics). Typical energy at each level: producers 10,000 kJ → primary consumers 1,000 kJ → secondary consumers 100 kJ → tertiary consumers 10 kJ.

**Niches and competitive exclusion:** A fundamental niche is the full range of conditions and resources a species could theoretically use. A realized niche is what it actually uses given competition, predation, and other biotic interactions. Gause's competitive exclusion principle: two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely — the superior competitor will exclude the other. Resource partitioning (different feeding times, microhabitats, or prey sizes) allows coexistence.

**Species interactions — competition:** Interspecific competition (between species) drives natural selection, character displacement (evolutionary divergence of traits), and competitive exclusion. Intraspecific competition (within species) regulates population density and drives territoriality. Competition coefficients (alpha values) in the Lotka-Volterra model quantify competitive impact. When competition is weak, species may coexist through niche differentiation.

**Species interactions — predation and defence:** Predation regulates prey population size and drives co-evolutionary arms races. Prey defences: crypsis (camouflage blending with background), masquerade (resembling an unpalatable object), warning coloration (aposematism — bright colours signal toxicity), Batesian mimicry (harmless species mimics a harmful one), Müllerian mimicry (two harmful species share warning signals), and behavioral defences (flocking, burrowing, alarm calls). Predator strategies include ambush, pursuit, and cooperative hunting.

**Species interactions — herbivory and plant defences:** Herbivory removes plant biomass and can reduce fitness, but at low levels it stimulates compensatory growth (increased photosynthesis and tillering). Plant defences: mechanical (thorns, spines, prickles, tough cuticles); chemical (alkaloids like nicotine and caffeine, tannins that bind proteins, terpenes that disrupt insect metabolism, cyanogenic glycosides); indirect (extrafloral nectar rewards for predator ants that defend the plant). Some herbivores have adapted to detoxify plant chemicals (e.g., monarch butterflies sequester cardenolides from milkweed).

**Species interactions — symbiosis types:** Mutualism: both benefit — pollinators and flowers (co-evolved traits: tube-shaped flowers with long proboscis moths), mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots (fungi supply phosphorus, plants supply sugars), nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) and legume roots, clownfish and sea anemones. Commensalism: one benefits, other unaffected — epiphytic orchids on tree branches (gain light, no harm to tree), remora fish attached to sharks (feed on scraps), cattle egrets following grazing livestock. Parasitism: one benefits at expense of other — tapeworms in intestines, ticks on mammals, mistletoe on trees, parasitoid wasps laying eggs in caterpillars.

**10% rule and energy flow:** Lindeman's 10% rule states that approximately 10% of energy is transferred between trophic levels. The remaining ~90% is lost as metabolic heat (respiration), used for movement and growth, or passes to decomposers as undigested matter. This limits food chains to 4-5 trophic levels because higher levels would receive insufficient energy. An eagle at trophic level 4 receives only ~0.1% of the solar energy captured by grass at level 1.

**Biomagnification and ecosystem health:** Toxic substances that are persistent, fat-soluble, and biologically inactive accumulate in organisms and increase in concentration at higher trophic levels. DDT in aquatic ecosystems: phytoplankton (0.04 ppm) → zooplankton (0.23 ppm) → small fish (1.67 ppm) → large fish (25 ppm) → osprey (500+ ppm). The osprey population crashed in the 1960s due to eggshell thinning. Mercury from coal plants bioaccumulates in fish, causing neurological damage in humans who consume contaminated seafood.

**Ecosystem services framework:** Provisioning services: food (crops, fish, game), fresh water, timber, fuel wood, fibres, medicinal plants, genetic resources. Regulating services: climate regulation (carbon sequestration), flood mitigation (wetlands absorb floodwaters), pollination (insects pollinate 75% of crops), disease regulation (predators control pest populations), water purification. Supporting services: soil formation (weathering + organic matter), nutrient cycling (nitrogen fixation, decomposition), primary production (photosynthesis), habitat provision. Cultural services: recreation, ecotourism, spiritual values, aesthetic inspiration, educational research.

**Ecosystem resilience and disturbance:** Resilience is the capacity of an ecosystem to absorb disturbance and reorganise while retaining its essential function, structure, and feedbacks. Moderate disturbances (fire, flooding, windthrow) can increase biodiversity by creating patches in different successional stages. However, chronic disturbances (continuous deforestation, pollution, overgrazing) push ecosystems past thresholds (tipping points) into alternative stable states — e.g., a coral reef collapsing into an algae-dominated state that cannot recover without intervention.

**Ecological succession:** Primary succession begins on bare substrate with no soil (lava flows, retreating glaciers, new islands) — pioneer species are lichens and mosses that weather rock and build soil. Secondary succession occurs where soil remains after disturbance (fire, logging, abandoned farmland) — grasses and weeds colonise first, followed by shrubs and shade-intolerant trees, eventually reaching a climax community. In Nepal, successional sequences after shifting cultivation (jhum) follow: grasses → shrubs (Lantana) → pioneer trees (Alnus, Betula) → mature forest (Schima, Castanopsis).

**Biogeochemical cycles — carbon and nitrogen:** Carbon cycle: CO2 is fixed by photosynthesis into organic compounds, released by respiration and decomposition, stored in fossil fuels (combustion releases ancient carbon), and dissolved in oceans (forming carbonic acid, causing ocean acidification). Human activities add ~40 billion tonnes of CO2 annually. Nitrogen cycle: N2 (78% of atmosphere) is fixed by bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules, free-living Azotobacter, cyanobacteria), converted to nitrates by nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), taken up by plants, and returned to atmosphere by denitrifying bacteria. Fertiliser use has doubled global nitrogen fixation rates.

**Trophic cascades and keystone species:** A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance. Sea otters in kelp forests: when otters were hunted to near extinction, sea urchin populations exploded and devoured kelp forests, transforming productive ecosystems into 'urchin barrens.' In Nepal, the Bengal tiger is a keystone predator — its removal leads to overpopulation of herbivores (deer, boar), which overbrowse forest understory, reducing plant diversity and affecting species that depend on dense understory cover.

**Ecological footprint and human impact:** An ecological footprint measures the area of biologically productive land and water needed to produce the resources a population consumes and absorb its waste. The global average is ~2.7 hectares per person, but Earth only has ~1.6 hectares per person — humanity is using 1.7 planets' worth of resources. Nepal's per capita footprint (~0.8 ha) is below global average, but urban areas like Kathmandu Valley have much higher effective footprints due to resource imports.

**Niche construction and ecosystem engineering:** Organisms are not just shaped by their environment — they also modify it. beavers build dams that create ponds, flood forests, and transform entire landscapes. Earthworms engineer soil structure through burrowing and casting. Corals build reefs that support 25% of marine species. In Nepal, red pandas modify forest structure by selectively feeding on certain bamboo species, influencing regeneration patterns. These 'ecosystem engineers' create habitats for countless other species.
confusion:
❌ Ecology is the same as environmentalism.
✅ Ecology is a branch of biology — the scientific study of organism-environment interactions. Environmentalism is a social and political movement advocating for nature conservation. Ecology provides the evidence base for environmental policy, but ecologists can study ecosystems without being environmental activists, just as physicists study atoms without advocating for nuclear energy.

❌ Abiotic factors are unimportant compared to biotic factors.
✅ Abiotic factors are often the primary determinants of where organisms can live. Temperature and water availability control biome distribution globally — a cactus cannot survive in a tundra regardless of competition. In aquatic systems, dissolved oxygen, pH, and salinity often limit species distribution more than biotic interactions do. The fundamental niche is defined by abiotic tolerances.

❌ A habitat is the same as a niche.
✅ A habitat is where an organism lives — its 'address' (e.g., a tropical rainforest canopy). A niche is how it lives — its 'profession' (what it eats, when it forages, how it reproduces, its temperature tolerance). Two species can share a habitat (e.g., two warbler species in the same tree) but occupy different niches (feeding at different heights, eating different insects).

❌ Symbiosis always means a mutually beneficial relationship.
✅ In biology, symbiosis simply means 'living together' and encompasses three types: mutualism (both benefit, e.g., mycorrhizal fungi and roots), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected, e.g., epiphytic orchids on trees), and parasitism (one benefits at expense of other, e.g., tapeworms in intestines). The majority of symbiotic relationships in nature are parasitic, not mutualistic.

❌ The competitive exclusion principle means two species cannot coexist at all.
✅ The competitive exclusion principle (Gause's law) states that two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely — the competitively superior species will eventually exclude the other. However, in nature, species typically diverge in their niches through character displacement or resource partitioning (different feeding times, different microhabitats, different prey sizes), allowing coexistence. Complete niche overlap is rare in mature communities.

❌ All ecological pyramids are upright (triangle-shaped).
✅ Only the pyramid of energy is always upright because energy is lost as heat at every transfer (2nd law of thermodynamics). Pyramids of number can be inverted (one large tree supports thousands of insects). Pyramids of biomass can be inverted in aquatic ecosystems (a small standing crop of phytoplankton reproduces rapidly and supports a larger standing crop of zooplankton).

❌ Energy and nutrients flow the same way in ecosystems.
✅ Energy flows in one direction: sun → producers → consumers → decomposers → heat (lost, not recyclable). Nutrients cycle: dead organisms are decomposed, nutrients return to soil/water, and are taken up again by producers. This is why ecosystems need a constant energy input (sunlight) but do not need a constant nutrient input — they recycle the same atoms billions of times.
practice: Classify the following interactions as mutualism, commensalism, or parasitism: (a) cleaner fish removing parasites from a larger fish, (b) a tiger stealing a leopard's kill, (c) oxpecker birds eating ticks off a rhinoceros. *Solution:* (a) Mutualism — cleaner fish gets food; larger fish gets parasites removed (both benefit). (b) Kleptoparasitism (a form of competition) — tiger benefits (free meal); leopard loses (wasted energy) — not symbiotic as no close long-term association. (c) Mutualism — oxpecker gets food (ticks); rhinoceros gets pest removal (both benefit). Note: some debates exist about whether oxpeckers also pick wounds, making it closer to parasitism.

Draw a pond ecosystem diagram labeling all biotic and abiotic components. Identify at least three food chains within it and show where decomposers fit in. *Solution:* Biotic: phytoplankton (producers), Daphnia (primary consumer), small fish (secondary consumer), pike (tertiary consumer), frogs (omnivore), heron (apex predator), bacteria/fungi (decomposers). Abiotic: sunlight, water, dissolved O2, CO2, nitrates, phosphates, temperature, sediment. Three food chains: (1) Phytoplankton → Daphnia → small fish → pike → decomposers. (2) Algae → snail → frog → heron → decomposers. (3) Detritus → bacteria → insect larvae → fish → heron → decomposers. Decomposers operate at every level, breaking down dead matter from all trophic levels.

Explain why food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels, referencing the 10% rule and energy loss at each level. *Solution:* Starting with 10,000 kJ of solar energy captured by producers (trophic level 1): Level 2 (herbivores) receives ~1,000 kJ (10%). Level 3 (carnivores) receives ~100 kJ. Level 4 receives ~10 kJ. Level 5 would receive ~1 kJ — insufficient to sustain a viable population. Additionally, energy is lost as heat through respiration at every level (metabolic heat is irrecoverable), through undigested material (faeces), and through death (organisms die without being eaten, passing energy to decomposers). Since ecosystems cannot create new energy (only capture it), each successive level has less available, making 4-5 levels the practical maximum.

Compare and contrast the structural and functional aspects of a pond ecosystem versus a forest ecosystem. Which has higher biodiversity? Which has faster nutrient cycling? *Solution:* Structure — Pond: open water column, rooted and floating plants, benthic sediment layer, vertical zonation (littoral, limnetic, profun-dal). Forest: vertical stratification (emergent, canopy, understory, shrub, herb, forest floor), complex root systems, thick organic litter layer. Function — Pond: energy flow through aquatic food chains (phytoplankton → zooplankton → fish), rapid nutrient cycling (nutrients dissolve directly in water), seasonal turnover mixes oxygen and nutrients. Forest: energy flow through complex terrestrial food webs (leaves → insects → birds → predators), slower nutrient cycling (nutrients locked in biomass and soil organic matter), mycorrhizal networks connect trees. Biodiversity: Tropical forests have higher species richness per unit area. Nutrient cycling: Ponds have faster cycling due to direct water-mediated transport and microbial activity in sediment.

Describe how biomagnification of DDT affected bald eagle populations in the mid-20th century. What does this illustrate about ecosystem interconnectedness? *Solution:* DDT was widely sprayed from the 1940s-1960s. It entered waterways, was absorbed by phytoplankton (0.04 ppm), concentrated in zooplankton (0.23 ppm), then small fish (1.67 ppm), large fish (25 ppm), and finally bald eagles (500+ ppm) that ate contaminated fish. DDT disrupted calcium metabolism, causing eggshells to be 20% thinner — eggs broke during incubation. Bald eagle populations declined from ~400,000 (1900) to 417 nesting pairs (1963) in the US. The 1972 DDT ban allowed recovery. This illustrates that chemicals applied on farmland can travel through food webs to affect apex predators hundreds of miles away — ecosystems are connected networks, not isolated boxes.

A student claims that 'decomposers are not part of the food chain.' Explain why this is incorrect and describe the role of decomposers in ecosystem function. *Solution:* Decomposers ARE fundamental parts of every food chain — they are the final trophic level that closes the loop. Without decomposers, dead organisms and waste would accumulate indefinitely, nutrients would remain locked in organic matter, and producers would run out of inorganic nutrients (N, P, K) needed for photosynthesis. In a food chain: grass → rabbit → fox → decomposers. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down the fox's dead body, releasing NH4+ (ammonium), PO43- (phosphate), and CO2 back into the soil and atmosphere, which grass roots and leaves can reabsorb. This nutrient recycling is the 'closing the loop' function that makes ecosystems sustainable. Detritivores (earthworms, millipedes) mechanically break down detritus, increasing surface area for microbial decomposition.

Calculate the energy available to a tertiary consumer if the producers capture 50,000 kJ of solar energy, assuming 10% transfer efficiency at each level. Show each step. *Solution:* Level 1 (producers): 50,000 kJ (given). Level 2 (primary consumer/herbivore): 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000 kJ. Level 3 (secondary consumer/carnivore): 5,000 × 0.10 = 500 kJ. Level 4 (tertiary consumer/top predator): 500 × 0.10 = 50 kJ. Only 50 kJ (0.1% of original solar energy) is available to the tertiary consumer. This demonstrates why top predators require large territories and why food chains are short — energy availability becomes limiting after 3-4 transfers.
universalFacts: Every ecosystem, regardless of size or location, requires three functional components: producers (to capture energy), consumers (to transfer energy), and decomposers (to recycle nutrients).
The Amazon rainforest produces approximately 20% of the world's oxygen and houses roughly 10% of all known species — demonstrating how biodiversity and ecosystem function are intertwined.

Ecologists use the term 'biome' to describe large-scale communities of organisms defined by climate and dominant vegetation. There are roughly 14 terrestrial biomes and 10 major aquatic biomes on Earth.
Eugene Odum's 1953 definition of ecology as 'the study of the structure and function of nature' remains one of the most widely cited definitions, emphasizing both organization and process.

Human activities now alter more than 75% of Earth's land surface and 66% of ocean area, making human ecology — the study of human impacts on ecosystems — one of the most important subfields of modern ecology.
